entries.meaning: Relating to Spain and Portugal, or the peninsula they share. ---
examples: Spain and Portugal make up the Iberian Peninsula.
The restaurant serves Iberian ham and cheese.
The architecture of the old mission is clearly Iberian.

entries.meaning: Ice-cold has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Nothing beats an ice-cold lemonade in July.
The water in the lake was ice-cold.
My hands were ice-cold after shoveling snow.
She gave him an ice-cold stare.
The kicker was ice-cold in the final seconds.

senses.head: Extremely cold
examples: Nothing beats an ice-cold lemonade in July.
The water in the lake was ice-cold.
My hands were ice-cold after shoveling snow.

senses.head: Showing no emotion or friendliness; calm under pressure
examples: She gave him an ice-cold stare.
The kicker was ice-cold in the final seconds.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: already ice-cold, not very ice-cold

entries.meaning: From or relating to Iceland, its people or its language. ---
examples: We tried Icelandic yogurt on our trip.
The band is Icelandic.
Icelandic horses are small but very strong.
entries.contrast: Always a capital letter. The language is Icelandic (noun); a person is an Icelander.

entries.meaning: Informal: unpleasant, sticky or disgusting. ---
examples: There's something icky on the bottom of my shoe.
The whole situation made me feel icky.
That was the ickiest bathroom I've ever seen.
entries.contrast: Informal and childish-sounding; adults use it for mild disgust or discomfort.

entries.meaning: Very famous and seen as a symbol of a time, place or idea. ---
examples: The Golden Gate Bridge is an iconic landmark.
Her red dress in the film became iconic.
It's one of the most iconic photos of the twentieth century.
entries.contrast: Not иконный: iconic means very famous and seen as a symbol of something.

entries.meaning: Attacking or rejecting accepted beliefs and traditions. ---
examples: He was an iconoclastic filmmaker who broke every rule.
Her ideas about economics were considered iconoclastic.
The band's second album was even more iconoclastic.
entries.form: -ic from iconoclast (a person who attacks accepted beliefs)

entries.meaning: Icy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Drive slowly — the roads are icy.
She slipped on the icy sidewalk.
An icy wind blew off the lake.
January is the iciest month in Chicago.
He gave me an icy stare.
Her voice was polite but icy.

senses.head: Covered with ice
examples: Drive slowly — the roads are icy.
She slipped on the icy sidewalk.

senses.head: Extremely cold
examples: An icy wind blew off the lake.
January is the iciest month in Chicago.

senses.head: Unfriendly and showing no warm feelings
examples: He gave me an icy stare.
Her voice was polite but icy.

entries.meaning: Ideal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This park is ideal for a picnic.
She's the ideal candidate for the job.
The weather was ideal for sailing.
In an ideal world, nobody would go hungry.
The ideal family on TV has nothing to do with real life.

senses.head: Perfect, or the best possible for a purpose
examples: This park is ideal for a picnic.
She's the ideal candidate for the job.
The weather was ideal for sailing.

senses.head: Existing only in the imagination, not in reality
examples: In an ideal world, nobody would go hungry.
The ideal family on TV has nothing to do with real life.

entries.comparison: not gradable — already means 'the best'; more ideal is heard in speech but avoided in careful writing
entries.contrast: an ideal is also a noun (a principle). In an ideal world means 'if things were perfect', which they are not.

entries.meaning: Believing that very good things are possible, often without being practical. ---
examples: She was a young, idealistic teacher who wanted to change the world.
His plan is idealistic, but it will never work.
I was more idealistic in college.

entries.meaning: Shown or imagined as better than it really is. ---
examples: The movie paints an idealized picture of small-town life.
Her memories of childhood are a little idealized.
Ads show a more idealized version of motherhood than real life does.

entries.meaning: Exactly the same. ---
examples: Mark and Mike are identical twins.
Your answer is identical to the one in the book.
The two houses look almost identical.
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: almost identical, nearly identical

entries.meaning: Able to be recognized or named. ---
examples: The paramedics were easily identifiable by their uniforms.
The report removed all identifiable information about patients.
The newer logo is more identifiable from a distance.

entries.meaning: Based on a set of political or social beliefs. ---
examples: The two parties have deep ideological differences.
The Cold War was an ideological struggle.
His objections were ideological, not practical.

entries.meaning: Sounding natural, the way a native speaker would say it. ---
examples: Her English is fluent and idiomatic.
The translation is accurate, but it isn't very idiomatic.
"I'm good" is a more idiomatic answer than "I am well" in casual speech.

entries.meaning: Unusual and typical of one particular person or thing. ---
examples: He has a very idiosyncratic way of dressing.
Her spelling is idiosyncratic, to say the least.
It's the most idiosyncratic museum I've ever visited.

entries.meaning: Very stupid. ---
examples: That was an idiotic thing to say.
I feel idiotic for believing him.
It's the most idiotic rule in the whole building.

entries.meaning: Idle has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Half the machines in the factory are idle.
The land has been sitting idle for years.
Thousands of idle workers are waiting for the strike to end.
The novel is about rich, idle young people in New York.
He never stays idle for long.
It was just idle gossip.
I asked out of idle curiosity.
Don't make idle threats to your kids.

senses.head: Not working or not being used
examples: Half the machines in the factory are idle.
The land has been sitting idle for years.
Thousands of idle workers are waiting for the strike to end.

senses.head: Lazy; spending time doing nothing useful
examples: The novel is about rich, idle young people in New York.
He never stays idle for long.

senses.head: Without real purpose or result
examples: It was just idle gossip.
I asked out of idle curiosity.
Don't make idle threats to your kids.

entries.position: both — idle gossip, threats and curiosity only before a noun
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like idol (кумир). To idle is also a verb: the engine idled.

entries.meaning: Extremely peaceful, beautiful and happy. ---
examples: They spent an idyllic summer at the lake.
The village looked idyllic under the snow.
It was the most idyllic spot we found on the whole trip.

entries.meaning: Iffy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The weather looks iffy for Saturday.
Our vacation plans are even iffier now that my boss said no.
That chicken smells a little iffy to me.
They bought the car from a pretty iffy dealer.

senses.head: Uncertain; not yet decided or known
examples: The weather looks iffy for Saturday.
Our vacation plans are even iffier now that my boss said no.

senses.head: Of doubtful quality, safety or honesty
examples: That chicken smells a little iffy to me.
They bought the car from a pretty iffy dealer.

entries.meaning: Making someone feel ashamed or lose respect in public. ---
examples: The season ended in an ignominious 40-point loss.
His exit from politics was quick and ignominious.
It was the most ignominious defeat in the team's history.

entries.meaning: Ignorant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He made some ignorant comments about immigrants.
People are often ignorant when it comes to mental illness.
I was more ignorant about politics at twenty than I like to admit.
Most voters are ignorant of the details of the bill.
She was completely ignorant about what her husband had done.

senses.head: Having little knowledge or education
examples: He made some ignorant comments about immigrants.
People are often ignorant when it comes to mental illness.
I was more ignorant about politics at twenty than I like to admit.

senses.head: Not knowing about a particular fact or situation
examples: Most voters are ignorant of the details of the bill.
She was completely ignorant about what her husband had done.

entries.form: -ant from ignore (in its old sense 'not know')
entries.contrast: Not 'ignoring': ignorant means not knowing. Someone who pays no attention on purpose ignores you.

entries.meaning: Uncomfortable, nervous or embarrassed. ---
examples: She felt ill at ease among his rich friends.
He looked ill at ease in a suit and tie.
I've never been more ill at ease than at that dinner.
entries.position: predicative only — never before a noun: an uncomfortable guest
entries.comparison: more/most — more ill at ease, most ill at ease
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with being sick: it means uncomfortable or nervous.

entries.meaning: Not sensible; likely to cause problems. ---
examples: Selling the house now would be an ill-advised move.
You'd be ill-advised to sign that contract without a lawyer.
It was the most ill-advised road trip we ever took.
entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also evaluative
entries.takes: to-infinitive — you would be ill-advised to...

entries.meaning: Badly planned from the start. ---
examples: The war was an ill-conceived adventure.
Critics say the new parking plan is ill-conceived.
It was one of the most ill-conceived marketing campaigns of the decade.
entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also evaluative

entries.meaning: Done or said without careful thought. ---
examples: He apologized for his ill-considered remarks.
The decision to cut the budget was hasty and ill-considered.
Few laws have been more ill-considered than this one.
entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also evaluative

entries.meaning: Not clearly described, marked or explained. ---
examples: My job has an ill-defined set of responsibilities.
The border between the two properties is ill-defined.
The goals of the project became even more ill-defined over time.
entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also quality

entries.meaning: Ill-equipped has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soldiers were ill-equipped for the winter.
Rural hospitals are often ill-equipped to treat serious burns.
Most parents feel ill-equipped to talk about drugs with their teenagers.
He was the most ill-equipped candidate for the job.

senses.head: Without the tools or supplies that are needed
examples: The soldiers were ill-equipped for the winter.
Rural hospitals are often ill-equipped to treat serious burns.

senses.head: Without the skills, knowledge or qualities needed to deal with something
examples: Most parents feel ill-equipped to talk about drugs with their teenagers.
He was the most ill-equipped candidate for the job.

entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also quality

entries.meaning: Ending badly, often in disaster or death. ---
examples: All 150 passengers on the ill-fated flight were killed.
The movie tells the story of an ill-fated expedition to the South Pole.
Their marriage seemed ill-fated from the start.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: the ill-fated flight

entries.meaning: Of clothes, shoes or parts, the wrong size or shape. ---
examples: He wore an ill-fitting suit to the interview.
Ill-fitting shoes can cause back pain.
The windows were old and ill-fitting, so the house was always cold.
entries.type: compound — adverb + present participle; also quality
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an ill-fitting suit

entries.meaning: Got in a dishonest or illegal way. ---
examples: The court ordered him to return his ill-gotten gains.
They lived for years on ill-gotten money from the scheme.
Police found the ill-gotten cash hidden in the garage.

entries.meaning: Rude; behaving badly toward other people. ---
examples: He's a loud, ill-mannered guest.
I didn't mean to be ill-mannered.
They were the most ill-mannered kids on the whole bus.

entries.meaning: Easily annoyed or angry; full of anger. ---
examples: The neighbors have an ill-tempered old dog.
The debate became ill-tempered within minutes.
He grew more ill-tempered as the day went on.

entries.meaning: Done or said at the wrong moment. ---
examples: His joke was badly ill-timed.
An ill-timed penalty cost them the game.
The price increase could not have been more ill-timed.
entries.type: compound — adverb + past participle; also evaluative

entries.meaning: Illegal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's illegal to text while driving in most states.
Police seized a large amount of illegal drugs.
Is it illegal to park here overnight?
The touchdown didn't count because of an illegal block.
Moving your king into check is an illegal move.

senses.head: Not allowed by law
examples: It's illegal to text while driving in most states.
Police seized a large amount of illegal drugs.
Is it illegal to park here overnight?

senses.head: In sports and games, against the rules
examples: The touchdown didn't count because of an illegal block.
Moving your king into check is an illegal move.

entries.meaning: Impossible or very hard to read because the writing is unclear. ---
examples: The doctor's handwriting is almost illegible.
The note was signed with an illegible scrawl.
The older letters were even more illegible than the new ones.
entries.contrast: Illegible is about letters you cannot make out. Unreadable can also mean too boring or badly written to read.

entries.meaning: Illegitimate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The opposition called the election illegitimate.
They refused to deal with an illegitimate government.
The king had several illegitimate children.
In those days, being illegitimate was a source of shame.

senses.head: Not allowed by law or rules, or not fair and acceptable
examples: The opposition called the election illegitimate.
They refused to deal with an illegitimate government.

senses.head: Born to parents who were not married to each other; now often considered old-fashioned
examples: The king had several illegitimate children.
In those days, being illegitimate was a source of shame.

entries.meaning: Not respecting free speech, individual rights or other people's views. ---
examples: Some elected leaders are building illiberal democracies.
Critics say the new law on protests is deeply illiberal.
The party has become more illiberal over the past decade.

entries.meaning: Illicit has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The police found illicit drugs in the trunk.
The border town is a center of illicit trade.
The senator admitted to an illicit affair.
There was something illicit about sneaking out after midnight.

senses.head: Not allowed by law
examples: The police found illicit drugs in the trunk.
The border town is a center of illicit trade.

senses.head: Not approved of by society and usually kept secret
examples: The senator admitted to an illicit affair.
There was something illicit about sneaking out after midnight.

entries.contrast: Sounds the same as the verb elicit (вызывать, добиваться ответа): elicit a response, but illicit drugs.

entries.meaning: Illiterate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His grandmother was illiterate and signed with an X.
The program teaches illiterate adults to read.
Millions of people in the region are still illiterate.
I'm completely computer illiterate.
Many young people are financially illiterate when they leave school.

senses.head: Unable to read or write
examples: His grandmother was illiterate and signed with an X.
The program teaches illiterate adults to read.
Millions of people in the region are still illiterate.

senses.head: Knowing very little about a particular subject
examples: I'm completely computer illiterate.
Many young people are financially illiterate when they leave school.

entries.comparison: not gradable — in the 'cannot read' sense; the 'knowing little' sense takes more/most

entries.meaning: Not reasonable or sensible; not following logic. ---
examples: His argument is completely illogical.
I know it's an illogical fear, but I hate flying.
The new rules are even more illogical than the old ones.

entries.meaning: Illuminated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: An illuminated sign pointed to the exit.
The bridge is illuminated at night.
The museum has a rare illuminated manuscript from the 1400s.
Monks spent years making illuminated Bibles.

senses.head: Lit up with light
examples: An illuminated sign pointed to the exit.
The bridge is illuminated at night.

senses.head: Of an old book or manuscript, decorated by hand with gold and colored pictures
examples: The museum has a rare illuminated manuscript from the 1400s.
Monks spent years making illuminated Bibles.

entries.meaning: Helping to explain something or making it easier to understand. ---
examples: The book offers an illuminating look at life in the 1930s.
Talking to the nurses was really illuminating.
It was the most illuminating lecture of the semester.
entries.form: -ing from illuminate — what makes something clear

entries.meaning: Seeming real or true but not actually so. ---
examples: The feeling of safety was illusory.
Many investors chased illusory profits.
The recovery turned out to be more illusory than real.

entries.meaning: Serving as an example that explains or shows something. ---
examples: Her story is illustrative of the problems many immigrants face.
The photos are for illustrative purposes only.
The most illustrative case is the one in Chapter 3.

entries.meaning: Famous and admired because of what someone has achieved. ---
examples: She had an illustrious career in the Senate.
The school's alumni list is long and illustrious.
He is one of the most illustrious scientists of his generation.

entries.meaning: Not having the right or equal amounts of different things. ---
examples: He eats a very imbalanced diet.
The trade relationship between the two countries is imbalanced.
The league has become more imbalanced since the rule change.
entries.contrast: Imbalanced is about unequal amounts. Unbalanced can also describe a mentally ill person.

entries.meaning: Made to look like something better or more expensive, and not the real thing. ---
examples: The bag is imitation leather.
They sell imitation crab meat by the pound.
The ring has an imitation diamond in it.
entries.contrast: Also a common noun (a good imitation). As an adjective it stands only before a noun: imitation leather, never the leather is imitation.

entries.meaning: Immaculate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her kitchen is always immaculate.
He showed up in an immaculate white shirt.
The pianist gave an immaculate performance.
The team's defense has been immaculate all season.

senses.head: Perfectly clean and neat
examples: Her kitchen is always immaculate.
He showed up in an immaculate white shirt.

senses.head: Without any mistakes; perfect
examples: The pianist gave an immaculate performance.
The team's defense has been immaculate all season.

entries.meaning: Immaterial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Whether he meant to do it is immaterial; the damage is done.
The cost is immaterial to me.
Many religions teach that the soul is immaterial.
Ghosts are usually imagined as immaterial beings.

senses.head: Not important or not relevant
examples: Whether he meant to do it is immaterial; the damage is done.
The cost is immaterial to me.

senses.head: Not having a physical form
examples: Many religions teach that the soul is immaterial.
Ghosts are usually imagined as immaterial beings.

entries.position: both — the 'not important' sense mostly after a verb: that's immaterial
entries.contrast: The everyday meaning is 'not important', not the Russian нематериальный, which is the rarer, formal sense.

entries.meaning: Immature has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Stop being so immature!
He's much more immature than his younger sister.
That was an immature thing to post online.
Immature birds have brown feathers.
A baby's immune system is still immature.

senses.head: Behaving in a childish way
examples: Stop being so immature!
He's much more immature than his younger sister.
That was an immature thing to post online.

senses.head: Not yet fully grown or developed
examples: Immature birds have brown feathers.
A baby's immune system is still immature.

entries.meaning: Too large or great to be measured. ---
examples: The storm caused immeasurable damage.
My debt to my teachers is immeasurable.
Her work brought immeasurable joy to millions of readers.

entries.meaning: Immediate has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The new manager made an immediate impact.
The effect of the medicine was immediate.
We need an immediate answer.
Only immediate family attended the funeral.
Residents in the immediate area were told to leave.
Our immediate concern is finding the missing child.
The shelter meets people's immediate needs for food and a bed.
The immediate cause of death was a heart attack.
She reports to her immediate supervisor.

senses.head: Happening or done at once, without delay
examples: The new manager made an immediate impact.
The effect of the medicine was immediate.
We need an immediate answer.

senses.head: Nearest in time, place or family relationship
examples: Only immediate family attended the funeral.
Residents in the immediate area were told to leave.

senses.head: Needing attention now; current
examples: Our immediate concern is finding the missing child.
The shelter meets people's immediate needs for food and a bed.

senses.head: Direct, with nothing in between
examples: The immediate cause of death was a heart attack.
She reports to her immediate supervisor.

entries.position: both — only the 'happening at once' sense after a verb; the others before a noun

entries.meaning: Extremely large or great. ---
examples: The project will cost an immense amount of money.
The pressure on the players is immense.
From the plane, the desert looked immense.
entries.comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: truly immense, rarely very immense

entries.meaning: About to happen very soon, usually something bad. ---
examples: Forecasters warned that a storm was imminent.
The old building is in imminent danger of collapse.
The threat is more imminent than officials are admitting.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with eminent (выдающийся): an eminent scientist, but imminent danger.

entries.meaning: Not moving, or unable to move. ---
examples: The deer stood immobile in the headlights.
After the accident, he was immobile for six weeks.
Nurses turn immobile patients every two hours.

entries.meaning: Morally wrong. ---
examples: Many people think it's immoral to charge that much for medicine.
The film was attacked as immoral when it came out.
What they did was even more immoral than breaking the law.
entries.contrast: Immoral means doing wrong. Amoral means having no idea of right and wrong at all.

entries.meaning: Immortal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The Greek gods were immortal.
Teenagers often act as if they're immortal.
In the immortal words of Yogi Berra, "It ain't over till it's over."
His best songs are truly immortal.

senses.head: Living forever
examples: The Greek gods were immortal.
Teenagers often act as if they're immortal.

senses.head: Famous or remembered forever
examples: In the immortal words of Yogi Berra, "It ain't over till it's over."
His best songs are truly immortal.

entries.meaning: Immovable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The piano was so heavy it was practically immovable.
What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object?
The union was immovable on the question of pay.
She became more immovable the harder they pushed.

senses.head: Impossible to move
examples: The piano was so heavy it was practically immovable.
What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object?

senses.head: Refusing to change an opinion or decision
examples: The union was immovable on the question of pay.
She became more immovable the harder they pushed.

entries.comparison: more/most — more immovable (the 'not changing your mind' sense); the physical sense is not gradable

entries.meaning: Immune has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Once you've had chickenpox, you're immune to it.
Some people seem naturally immune to the virus.
No business is immune to a recession.
Politicians become more immune to criticism the longer they stay in office.
Diplomats are immune from prosecution.
The witness was granted immune status in exchange for testimony.
Stress can weaken your immune system.
The vaccine triggers a strong immune response.

senses.head: Protected from a disease, so that you cannot catch it
examples: Once you've had chickenpox, you're immune to it.
Some people seem naturally immune to the virus.

senses.head: Not affected or influenced by something
examples: No business is immune to a recession.
Politicians become more immune to criticism the longer they stay in office.

senses.head: Protected from something bad, such as punishment or attack
examples: Diplomats are immune from prosecution.
The witness was granted immune status in exchange for testimony.

senses.head: Relating to the body's defense against disease
examples: Stress can weaken your immune system.
The vaccine triggers a strong immune response.

entries.position: both — the 'immune system' sense only before a noun
entries.takes: to + disease or influence; from + punishment, attack or prosecution
entries.contrast: Immune to a disease or to criticism; immune from prosecution or punishment.

entries.meaning: Having an immune system that is weak because of illness or medicine. ---
examples: Flu shots are especially important for immunocompromised patients.
My mother is immunocompromised because of her cancer treatment.
The hospital keeps immunocompromised children in a separate ward.

entries.meaning: Never changing or impossible to change. ---
examples: The laws of physics are immutable.
Few rules in politics are truly immutable.
Once written, the record is immutable and cannot be edited.

entries.meaning: Impacted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Aid is on its way to the impacted communities.
Workers in the impacted departments will be offered new jobs.
I had two impacted wisdom teeth pulled last week.
The X-ray showed the tooth was impacted.

senses.head: Affected by something, usually in a bad way
examples: Aid is on its way to the impacted communities.
Workers in the impacted departments will be offered new jobs.

senses.head: Of a tooth, stuck under the gum or another tooth and unable to grow out normally
examples: I had two impacted wisdom teeth pulled last week.
The X-ray showed the tooth was impacted.

entries.contrast: In the 'affected' sense, affected is still the safer word in formal writing; some editors object to impacted.

entries.meaning: Impaired has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her vision is impaired in one eye.
The program serves hearing-impaired students.
His memory was more impaired than the doctors first thought.
He was arrested for driving while impaired.
Impaired drivers cause thousands of deaths every year.

senses.head: Damaged or weakened, so that it does not work well
examples: Her vision is impaired in one eye.
The program serves hearing-impaired students.
His memory was more impaired than the doctors first thought.

senses.head: Less able to think or drive because of alcohol or drugs
examples: He was arrested for driving while impaired.
Impaired drivers cause thousands of deaths every year.

entries.meaning: Not favoring one side; fair. ---
examples: Judges must remain impartial.
We asked an impartial expert to review the data.
The new referee was more impartial than the last one.
entries.contrast: Partial means both 'incomplete' and 'biased'; impartial is only the opposite of 'biased'.

entries.meaning: Impossible to travel along or through. ---
examples: Heavy snow made the mountain roads impassable.
The trail is impassable after a storm.
Floods turned the valley into an impassable swamp.

entries.meaning: Showing strong feeling. ---
examples: The mother made an impassioned plea for her son's release.
The debate in Congress was long and impassioned.
It was the most impassioned speech of her career.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an impassioned speech
entries.contrast: Looks like impassive, but means the opposite: impassioned is full of feeling, impassive shows none.

entries.meaning: Not showing any emotion. ---
examples: The defendant remained impassive as the verdict was read.
The guard stared at us with an impassive face.
She was the most impassive poker player at the table.
entries.contrast: Looks like impassioned, but means the opposite: impassive shows no feeling.

entries.meaning: Impatient has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't be so impatient with your little brother.
The impatient driver behind us kept honking.
I get more impatient at the airport every year.
The kids were impatient to open their presents.
Voters are impatient for change.

senses.head: Easily annoyed, especially when you have to wait
examples: Don't be so impatient with your little brother.
The impatient driver behind us kept honking.
I get more impatient at the airport every year.

senses.head: Wanting something to happen very soon
examples: The kids were impatient to open their presents.
Voters are impatient for change.

entries.takes: with + person; at or with + situation; for + noun; to-infinitive

entries.meaning: Perfect, with no faults or mistakes. ---
examples: She has impeccable taste in clothes.
His manners were impeccable.
The restaurant has the most impeccable service in town.

entries.meaning: About to happen, usually something unpleasant. ---
examples: Residents were warned of the impending hurricane.
I had a sense of impending doom.
News of the impending layoffs spread quickly.

entries.meaning: Impenetrable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The jungle was thick and impenetrable.
The fortress had impenetrable stone walls.
The contract is written in impenetrable legal language.
His later novels are even more impenetrable.

senses.head: Impossible to get through, into or see through
examples: The jungle was thick and impenetrable.
The fortress had impenetrable stone walls.

senses.head: Impossible to understand
examples: The contract is written in impenetrable legal language.
His later novels are even more impenetrable.

entries.meaning: So small or slight that it can hardly be noticed. ---
examples: She gave an almost imperceptible nod.
The change in temperature was imperceptible.
The difference between the two versions is nearly imperceptible.

entries.meaning: Having faults or weaknesses; not perfect. ---
examples: We live in an imperfect world.
The system is imperfect, but it's the best we have.
The store sells imperfect fruit at a discount.

entries.meaning: Imperial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We toured the imperial palace in Beijing.
Rome's imperial power lasted for centuries.
The country still struggles with its imperial past.
The recipe gives both metric and imperial measurements.
American tools still use imperial sizes.

senses.head: Relating to an empire or an emperor
examples: We toured the imperial palace in Beijing.
Rome's imperial power lasted for centuries.
The country still struggles with its imperial past.

senses.head: Of units of measure, belonging to the non-metric system of inches, pounds and gallons
examples: The recipe gives both metric and imperial measurements.
American tools still use imperial sizes.

entries.meaning: Supporting or relating to one country's control over other countries. ---
examples: The protesters condemned imperialist wars.
The novel is a critique of imperialist attitudes.
Critics called the plan openly imperialist.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an imperialist is a person who supports empire.

entries.meaning: Expecting others to obey you, in a proud and unfriendly way. ---
examples: She waved the waiter over with an imperious gesture.
Her tone was cold and imperious.
He grew more imperious after his promotion.

entries.meaning: Not allowing liquid or gas to pass through. ---
examples: The jacket is made of an impermeable fabric.
Clay soil is nearly impermeable to water.
The new coating is more impermeable than the old one.

entries.meaning: Impersonal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hotel was clean but very impersonal.
Big hospitals can feel cold and impersonal.
Email is a more impersonal way to deliver bad news.
It seems that is an impersonal construction.
Russian uses impersonal sentences much more than English does.

senses.head: Not friendly or warm; without personal feeling
examples: The hotel was clean but very impersonal.
Big hospitals can feel cold and impersonal.
Email is a more impersonal way to deliver bad news.

senses.head: In grammar, having no real subject, like it in it is raining
examples: It seems that is an impersonal construction.
Russian uses impersonal sentences much more than English does.

entries.meaning: Rude and not showing proper respect. ---
examples: Forgive me if this is an impertinent question.
The boy was sent home for being impertinent to his teacher.
Her replies became more impertinent as the interview went on.
entries.contrast: Looks like 'not pertinent', but it almost always means rude. For 'not relevant' say irrelevant.

entries.meaning: Impervious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He seems impervious to criticism.
She was more impervious to the cold than the rest of us.
The roof is covered with an impervious layer of rubber.
Paved surfaces are impervious to rain, which causes flooding.

senses.head: Not affected or influenced by something
examples: He seems impervious to criticism.
She was more impervious to the cold than the rest of us.

senses.head: Not allowing water or other substances to pass through
examples: The roof is covered with an impervious layer of rubber.
Paved surfaces are impervious to rain, which causes flooding.

entries.meaning: Acting quickly without thinking about the results. ---
examples: It was an impetuous decision, and she regretted it.
He was young and impetuous.
She was the most impetuous of the three sisters.

entries.meaning: Playfully naughty. ---
examples: He gave me an impish grin.
Her sense of humor is a little impish.
The younger twin was always the more impish one.

entries.meaning: Impossible to calm down, satisfy or stop. ---
examples: The two men were implacable enemies.
Her opposition to the plan was implacable.
He was the most implacable critic the governor ever had.

entries.meaning: Difficult to believe; not likely to be true. ---
examples: His excuse sounded implausible.
The movie has a totally implausible plot.
Each new explanation was more implausible than the last.

entries.meaning: Implicit has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There was an implicit threat in his words.
The right to privacy is implicit in the Constitution.
The message was more implicit in the first version of the ad.
She has implicit trust in her doctor.
Soldiers are expected to show implicit obedience.

senses.head: Suggested or understood without being said directly
examples: There was an implicit threat in his words.
The right to privacy is implicit in the Constitution.
The message was more implicit in the first version of the ad.

senses.head: Complete and without any doubt
examples: She has implicit trust in her doctor.
Soldiers are expected to show implicit obedience.

entries.position: both — the 'complete' sense only before a noun: implicit trust
entries.takes: in + noun — implicit in the agreement

entries.meaning: Asking for something in a desperate or emotional way. ---
examples: The dog gave me an imploring look.
Her voice was soft and imploring.
His letters grew more imploring each week.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an imploring look

entries.meaning: Not polite; rude. ---
examples: It's impolite to talk with your mouth full.
I didn't want to seem impolite to her parents.
Checking your phone at dinner is more impolite than being late.
entries.takes: to + person; to-infinitive — it's impolite to...

entries.meaning: Brought in from another country to be sold. ---
examples: The store sells imported cheeses from France and Italy.
Imported cars used to be much more expensive.
Most of the steel used here is imported.

entries.meaning: Large, impressive and making people feel respect. ---
examples: The bank is an imposing stone building on Main Street.
At six foot six, he was an imposing figure.
The mountains looked even more imposing up close.
entries.contrast: Not related to impose on (навязывать): an imposing building or person is big and impressive.

entries.meaning: Impotent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The UN seemed impotent in the face of the crisis.
I felt impotent rage as I watched them tow my car.
The committee is more impotent than ever.
Some blood pressure drugs can make men impotent.
He was afraid he would become impotent after the surgery.

senses.head: Without the power to change or control a situation
examples: The UN seemed impotent in the face of the crisis.
I felt impotent rage as I watched them tow my car.
The committee is more impotent than ever.

senses.head: Of a man, unable to have sex because he cannot get an erection
examples: Some blood pressure drugs can make men impotent.
He was afraid he would become impotent after the surgery.

entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable: IM-puh-tuhnt, not im-POH-tent, even though potent is POH-tuhnt.

entries.meaning: Impoverished has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She grew up in an impoverished neighborhood in Detroit.
It is one of the most impoverished countries in the world.
The war left the region impoverished.
Crops grow poorly in impoverished soil.
Without art and music, our schools would be culturally impoverished.

senses.head: Very poor
examples: She grew up in an impoverished neighborhood in Detroit.
It is one of the most impoverished countries in the world.
The war left the region impoverished.

senses.head: Made weaker or worse in quality, because something important is missing
examples: Crops grow poorly in impoverished soil.
Without art and music, our schools would be culturally impoverished.

entries.meaning: Impractical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: White carpets are impractical if you have kids.
The plan is too expensive and impractical.
High heels are the most impractical shoes for a hike.
My father was a brilliant but impractical man.
Artists are often accused of being impractical.

senses.head: Not sensible or not easy to use or do in real life
examples: White carpets are impractical if you have kids.
The plan is too expensive and impractical.
High heels are the most impractical shoes for a hike.

senses.head: Of a person, not good at dealing with ordinary practical matters
examples: My father was a brilliant but impractical man.
Artists are often accused of being impractical.

entries.meaning: Not exact or accurate. ---
examples: The law uses imprecise language that confuses everyone.
Weather forecasts for next month are still imprecise.
Older methods of dating fossils were far more imprecise.

entries.meaning: Impregnable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The castle was built to be impregnable.
It was once the most impregnable fortress in Europe.
By halftime the team had an impregnable lead.
The senator's position in the party seemed impregnable.

senses.head: Of a building or place, too strong to be captured or entered
examples: The castle was built to be impregnable.
It was once the most impregnable fortress in Europe.

senses.head: Too strong to be defeated or weakened
examples: By halftime the team had an impregnable lead.
The senator's position in the party seemed impregnable.

entries.contrast: Nothing to do with pregnant: it comes from a Latin word meaning 'to take'.

entries.meaning: Feeling admiration for someone or something. ---
examples: I was really impressed by her English.
The judges were impressed with his cooking.
My parents were more impressed with the house than I was.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: we were impressed
entries.form: -ed from impress — how the person feels
entries.contrast: -ed/-ing trap: you are impressed; the thing that makes you feel that way is impressive.

entries.meaning: Easily influenced by other people, especially because young. ---
examples: The show isn't suitable for impressionable teenagers.
She moved to the city at an impressionable age.
Younger kids are even more impressionable than teens.

entries.meaning: Impressionistic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The report gives only an impressionistic picture of the problem.
Her memories of the war are vague and impressionistic.
He paints impressionistic landscapes of the Maine coast.
The film's second half is more impressionistic than the first.

senses.head: Based on general feelings and impressions rather than exact facts or details
examples: The report gives only an impressionistic picture of the problem.
Her memories of the war are vague and impressionistic.

senses.head: In the style of Impressionism, using light and color rather than exact detail
examples: He paints impressionistic landscapes of the Maine coast.
The film's second half is more impressionistic than the first.

entries.meaning: Causing admiration because it is very good, large or skillful. ---
examples: She has an impressive resume.
The view from the top is really impressive.
It was the most impressive performance of the night.
entries.form: -ive from impress — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: -ed/-ing trap: the thing is impressive; the person who admires it is impressed.

entries.meaning: Kept in prison, or trapped somewhere you cannot leave. ---
examples: The group is fighting for the release of imprisoned journalists.
Families of imprisoned protesters gathered outside the court.
During the lockdown, she felt imprisoned in her tiny apartment.

entries.meaning: Not likely to happen or be true. ---
examples: It seems improbable that he did it alone.
The team made an improbable comeback in the last minute.
It was the most improbable friendship I've ever seen.

entries.meaning: Done or made without planning or preparation. ---
examples: The band gave an impromptu concert in the parking lot.
We had an impromptu meeting in the hallway.
His speech was completely impromptu.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an impromptu party
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (she spoke impromptu) and a noun for a short piece of music; only the adjective is shown here.

entries.meaning: Improper has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The official was fired for improper use of public funds.
Improper storage can cause food to spoil.
Nothing improper happened, the investigation found.
He was accused of improper behavior toward a student.
It would be improper for a judge to accept such a gift.

senses.head: Not correct, legal or following the rules
examples: The official was fired for improper use of public funds.
Improper storage can cause food to spoil.
Nothing improper happened, the investigation found.

senses.head: Not socially acceptable, especially in a sexual way
examples: He was accused of improper behavior toward a student.
It would be improper for a judge to accept such a gift.

entries.meaning: Better than before. ---
examples: The company released an improved version of the app.
His grades are much improved this year.
She won the award for most improved player.

entries.meaning: Improvised has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Most of the dialogue in the movie was improvised.
The comedy club has improvised shows every Friday.
The hikers slept in an improvised shelter of branches.
The soldiers were hit by an improvised explosive device.

senses.head: Done or performed without preparation
examples: Most of the dialogue in the movie was improvised.
The comedy club has improvised shows every Friday.

senses.head: Made quickly from whatever materials are available
examples: The hikers slept in an improvised shelter of branches.
The soldiers were hit by an improvised explosive device.

entries.meaning: Not sensible or careful, especially about the future. ---
examples: It would be imprudent to spend all your savings on a car.
The bank made several imprudent loans.
Nothing could be more imprudent than signing without reading.
entries.takes: to-infinitive — it would be imprudent to...

entries.meaning: Rude and not showing respect, often in a bold way. ---
examples: The teacher had no patience for impudent students.
Don't be impudent, young man!
His answers got more impudent with every question.

entries.meaning: Acting suddenly without thinking carefully first. ---
examples: Stores put candy near the checkout to encourage impulsive buying.
He's smart but a little impulsive.
Teenagers are often more impulsive than adults.

entries.meaning: Impure has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The impure water made several people sick.
Cheap gold jewelry is often impure.
The preacher warned against impure thoughts.
In the story, the priest believed his motives were impure.

senses.head: Mixed with other substances, usually of lower quality
examples: The impure water made several people sick.
Cheap gold jewelry is often impure.

senses.head: Morally bad, especially in a sexual way; used mainly in religious language
examples: The preacher warned against impure thoughts.
In the story, the priest believed his motives were impure.

entries.meaning: Between two stages, sizes or kinds; not clearly one or the other. ---
examples: My hair is at that awkward in-between length.
Twelve is a tough in-between age.
The color isn't blue or green; it's sort of in-between.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an in-between stage
entries.contrast: Without a hyphen, in between is an adverb or preposition: a table in between the chairs.

entries.meaning: Done with people physically present, not online or by phone. ---
examples: The school returned to in-person classes in the fall.
I prefer in-person meetings to video calls.
The second round is an in-person interview.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the adverb phrase in person
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is hyphenated: an in-person interview. After a verb there is no hyphen: we met in person.

entries.meaning: Deliberately bold or aggressive, in a way that is hard to ignore. ---
examples: The ad campaign is loud and in-your-face.
He has an in-your-face style of comedy.
Their new album is even more in-your-face than the last one.
entries.type: compound — phrase used as an adjective; also quality

entries.meaning: Inaccessible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The village is inaccessible by car in winter.

The most inaccessible parts of the park can only be reached by boat.
Much modern poetry is inaccessible to the average reader.
The lecture was interesting but a bit inaccessible.

senses.head: Hard or impossible to reach, enter or use
examples: The village is inaccessible by car in winter.
The old train station is inaccessible to wheelchair users.
The most inaccessible parts of the park can only be reached by boat.

senses.head: Too difficult for ordinary people to understand or enjoy
examples: Much modern poetry is inaccessible to the average reader.
The lecture was interesting but a bit inaccessible.

entries.meaning: Not correct or exact. ---
examples: The article contains several inaccurate statements.
The old map turned out to be inaccurate.
The early polls were even more inaccurate than usual.

entries.meaning: Inactive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Sitting at a desk all day leaves you inactive for hours at a time.
Inactive dogs put on weight fast.
He is even more inactive now than he was last winter.
Your account has been inactive for six months.
The volcano has been inactive since 1957.

senses.head: Not moving around or getting any exercise
examples: Sitting at a desk all day leaves you inactive for hours at a time.
Inactive dogs put on weight fast.
He is even more inactive now than he was last winter.

senses.head: Not working, not in use, or no longer taking part
examples: Your account has been inactive for six months.
The volcano has been inactive since 1957.

entries.meaning: Inadequate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The funding is inadequate for a school this size.
Our old wiring proved inadequate.
The second plan was even more inadequate than the first.
Her comments made me feel inadequate.
He always felt inadequate next to his older brother.

senses.head: Not enough, or not good enough for what is needed
examples: The funding is inadequate for a school this size.
Our old wiring proved inadequate.
The second plan was even more inadequate than the first.

senses.head: Feeling that you are not good enough
examples: Her comments made me feel inadequate.
He always felt inadequate next to his older brother.

entries.contrast: A false friend. Russian «неадекватный» usually means unreasonable or out of control; English inadequate means not enough or not good enough.

entries.meaning: Not allowed to be used, especially as evidence in a court. ---
examples: The judge ruled the confession inadmissible.
Inadmissible evidence never reaches the jury.
Anything found in that search is legally inadmissible.

entries.meaning: Done by accident, without meaning to. ---
examples: One inadvertent click sent the email to the whole company.
The damage was inadvertent, but it was still expensive.
Most of these errors are inadvertent.

entries.meaning: Not a wise thing to do. ---
examples: It is inadvisable to drive in fog like this.
Changing the plan now would be inadvisable.
The doctor said surgery was inadvisable at his age.
entries.position: predicative only — usually it is inadvisable to

entries.meaning: Belonging to someone in a way that cannot be taken away. ---
examples: Voting is an inalienable right of every citizen.
The treaty speaks of the inalienable rights of every people.
They regard clean water as an inalienable right.
entries.contrast: Almost always with right or rights. The Declaration of Independence spells it unalienable.

entries.meaning: Silly and completely without meaning. ---
examples: He made some inane comment about my haircut.
The questions got more inane as the interview went on.
I can't sit through another hour of inane chatter.

entries.meaning: Not alive; not a living creature. ---
examples: A rock is an inanimate object.
Small children talk to inanimate things all the time.
In that painting even the furniture hardly looks inanimate.
entries.contrast: Grammar uses the word too: an inanimate noun takes it, not he or she.

entries.meaning: Not relevant to a particular case or group. ---
examples: The rule is inapplicable to part-time staff.

The court found the old statute inapplicable.

entries.meaning: Not right for the occasion, the person or the place. ---

entries.meaning: Unable to say clearly what you mean, or not said clearly. ---

I felt more inarticulate with every question they asked.

entries.meaning: Not watching or listening carefully enough. ---
examples: The waiter was friendly but inattentive.
Inattentive drivers cause most of these crashes.
He grew more inattentive as the lecture went on.

entries.meaning: Too quiet to be heard. ---
examples: His voice was almost inaudible over the traffic.

The last word on the recording is inaudible.
entries.comparison: not gradable — softened instead: almost inaudible

entries.meaning: First of its kind, or marking the start of something. ---
examples: She gave her inaugural speech on a freezing January morning.
The team plays its inaugural game in April.

entries.contrast: Also a noun: the inaugural is the ceremony itself.

entries.meaning: Suggesting that what follows will go badly. ---
examples: It was an inauspicious start to the season.

entries.meaning: Not genuine, or not true to what it claims to be. ---

entries.meaning: Present in a person from birth rather than learned. ---

entries.meaning: Coming in toward a place, rather than leaving it. ---
examples: All inbound flights are delayed by the storm.

entries.meaning: Inbred has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The herd is badly inbred.

Her politeness is inbred.

senses.head: Bred from parents that are close relatives
examples: The herd is badly inbred.
Inbred mice are standard in lab research.

senses.head: Deep in someone since childhood, almost part of their nature
examples: He has an inbred distrust of banks.
Her politeness is inbred.

entries.meaning: Too great or too complicated to be measured. ---
examples: The storm did incalculable damage to the coast.

War causes incalculable human suffering.

entries.meaning: Of the Inca people who ruled the Andes before the Spanish came. ---
examples: They hiked four days to the Incan ruins.
The museum has a room of Incan gold.
Incan roads crossed the whole empire.
entries.contrast: Often written Inca instead: Inca ruins, Incan ruins — both are used.

entries.meaning: Giving off light because it is heated until it glows. ---
examples: Old incandescent bulbs waste most of their energy as heat.
The steel came out of the furnace white and incandescent.
He replaced every incandescent fixture with LEDs.
entries.contrast: Incandescent with rage (furious) is mainly British; Americans say livid.

entries.meaning: Not able to do something at all. ---
examples: He is incapable of lying.

entries.position: predicative only — incapable of + noun or -ing
entries.contrast: Incapable of doing — never incapable to do. It is unable that takes the to-infinitive.

entries.meaning: Unable to act or function normally, usually through injury or illness. ---

entries.meaning: Held in a prison or jail. ---

entries.contrast: Formal, and standard in American news writing: incarcerated people rather than inmates.

entries.meaning: Incendiary has 2 distinct senses.

Nothing he wrote was more incendiary than that last paragraph.

senses.head: Made to start a fire
examples: Incendiary bombs destroyed most of the old city.
The fire was set with a homemade incendiary device.

senses.head: Likely to stir up anger or violence
examples: His speech was deliberately incendiary.
The article made some incendiary claims about the mayor.
Nothing he wrote was more incendiary than that last paragraph.

entries.contrast: Also a noun: an incendiary is a fire bomb, or a person who stirs up trouble.

entries.meaning: Extremely angry. ---
examples: Parents were incensed by the decision.

entries.contrast: The noun incense — scented smoke — is stressed on the first syllable and is a different word.

entries.meaning: Going on and on without stopping. ---
examples: The incessant barking next door kept me up all night.

Her questions were incessant.
entries.form: in- + a Latin form of cease — literally not ceasing

entries.meaning: Incestuous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The novel deals with an incestuous relationship.

Publishing can feel like an incestuous little world.
No industry is more incestuous than this one.

senses.head: Involving sex between close relatives
examples: The novel deals with an incestuous relationship.
Incestuous marriage is illegal in every state.

senses.head: So closed that the same small group deals only with itself
examples: The city's political scene is famously incestuous.
Publishing can feel like an incestuous little world.
No industry is more incestuous than this one.

entries.meaning: Happening alongside something more important; minor. ---
examples: The grant covers travel, meals and incidental costs.

entries.contrast: Incidental music is the background music of a play or film. The adverb incidentally means 'by the way'.

entries.meaning: Just beginning, and not yet easy to see. ---
examples: Doctors caught the incipient infection early.

entries.contrast: Formal. Everyday English says early or just starting.

entries.meaning: Getting straight to the heart of a matter, in a clear and sharp way. ---
examples: She asked two incisive questions and the whole case fell apart.
His commentary is incisive without being cruel.
The second essay is far more incisive than the first.
entries.form: -ive from the Latin for cut into

entries.meaning: Cold, wet or stormy. ---
examples: The game was called off because of inclement weather.

entries.contrast: Used almost only of weather, and mostly in announcements and official notices.

entries.meaning: Inclined has 3 distinct senses.

senses.head: Feeling that you want to do something, or likely to do it
examples: I am inclined to agree with her.
He is inclined to exaggerate when he tells that story.

senses.head: Having a natural talent for or interest in something
examples: Their daughter is musically inclined.
The class is for students who are more technically inclined.

senses.head: Sloping rather than flat or upright

senses.head: Deliberately open to everyone, leaving no group out
examples: The new hiring policy is meant to be more inclusive.
She runs an inclusive classroom where nobody sits alone.
It is the most inclusive club on campus.

senses.head: Containing everything mentioned, with nothing charged on top
examples: The price is inclusive of tax and tips.
The course runs June 3 to June 14 inclusive.

entries.contrast: In dates and page ranges it follows the noun: Monday through Friday inclusive.

entries.meaning: Hiding who you really are, usually under another name. ---
examples: The singer was incognito in a baseball cap and sunglasses.
For two weeks he stayed incognito in a small hotel.
She prefers to remain incognito at these events.
entries.contrast: More often an adverb: she travels incognito. As an adjective it only follows a verb — never an incognito actor.

entries.meaning: Not making sense, because the parts do not hang together. ---
examples: He was so tired that he was incoherent by midnight.

entries.meaning: Incoming has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Coming in or arriving
examples: The phone blocks incoming calls from unknown numbers.
Incoming freshmen move in on Saturday.

senses.head: About to take over a job or an office from someone else
examples: The incoming mayor takes office in January.
The incoming class of senators is unusually young.

entries.meaning: Cut off from talking to anyone outside, by choice or by force. ---
examples: The prisoner was held incommunicado for three weeks.
He goes incommunicado whenever he is finishing a book.
The crew stayed incommunicado until the mission ended.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: held incommunicado. Never before a noun.

entries.meaning: So good that nothing else comes close. ---
examples: The view from the ridge is incomparable.
She was an incomparable teacher of young children.
His timing as a comedian is incomparable.
entries.contrast: The stress moves off compare: in-KAHM-pur-uh-buhl, not in-kum-PAIR-uh-buhl.

entries.meaning: Unable to work, exist or live together. ---
examples: The old printer is incompatible with this laptop.

The two accounts of the evening are more incompatible the closer you read them.

entries.meaning: Not able to do a job properly. ---
examples: The contractor turned out to be completely incompetent.
An incompetent manager can ruin a good team.
He is the most incompetent driver I have ever ridden with.
entries.contrast: In law it also means unfit to stand trial or to manage your own affairs: ruled mentally incompetent.

entries.meaning: Missing a part, or not finished. ---
examples: The application is incomplete without a signature.
We have only incomplete records from before 1940.
His third pass of the night was incomplete.
entries.contrast: In American schools an incomplete is also a noun: a grade that says the work is not finished yet.

entries.meaning: Impossible to understand. ---
examples: The instructions are incomprehensible to anyone but an engineer.
He left an incomprehensible voicemail at two in the morning.
Her decision to quit is incomprehensible to the rest of us.

entries.meaning: So unlikely or so strange that you cannot imagine it. ---
examples: It is inconceivable that nobody noticed the money was gone.
