Fifty years ago the idea was inconceivable.

entries.meaning: Not leading to a clear answer or result. ---
examples: The blood test came back inconclusive.
After three hours of inconclusive talks, they went home.
The second round of results was even more inconclusive.

entries.meaning: Out of place next to everything around it. ---
examples: A glass tower looks incongruous on that old street.
There was something incongruous about a tuxedo at a picnic.
Nothing could be more incongruous than palm trees in Ohio.

entries.meaning: Too small or minor to matter. ---
examples: We argued for an hour over something inconsequential.
The changes to the contract are inconsequential.
His objection was the most inconsequential of the three.

entries.meaning: Not thinking about how your behavior affects other people. ---
examples: Playing music at 3 a.m. is inconsiderate.
It was inconsiderate of him to cancel an hour before dinner.
Our new neighbors are even more inconsiderate than the last ones.
entries.takes: of + noun; to or toward + noun
entries.contrast: Not inconsiderable, a different word meaning small or not worth counting — usually met as the double negative not inconsiderable (= sizable).

entries.meaning: Inconsistent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His work is good but inconsistent.
The team has been inconsistent all season.
Her sleep got more inconsistent after the baby arrived.
His story is inconsistent with the security video.
The two reports are inconsistent on the date.

senses.head: Changing from one time to the next; not steady
examples: His work is good but inconsistent.
The team has been inconsistent all season.
Her sleep got more inconsistent after the baby arrived.

senses.head: Not matching something else, so that both cannot be true
examples: His story is inconsistent with the security video.
The two reports are inconsistent on the date.

entries.meaning: So sad that nothing anyone says helps. ---
examples: She was inconsolable for weeks after the funeral.
The little boy was inconsolable when the dog died.
His inconsolable grief frightened the whole family.

entries.meaning: Not easy to notice. ---
examples: The entrance is small and inconspicuous.
He tried to make himself inconspicuous at the back of the room.
A gray car is more inconspicuous than a red one.

entries.meaning: So clear that nobody can argue against it. ---
examples: The DNA evidence is incontestable.
She has an incontestable claim to the land.
That he saved the company is incontestable.

entries.meaning: Unable to control the bladder or bowels. ---
examples: After the stroke he was incontinent for several months.
The ward has special bedding for incontinent patients.
Many older dogs become incontinent.
entries.form: in- + continent in its old sense holding in
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with the noun continent (континент), though the two are spelled the same.

entries.meaning: Impossible to deny or disprove. ---
examples: The prosecution called the fingerprints incontrovertible.
There is now incontrovertible proof that the emails were edited.
The link between smoking and cancer is incontrovertible.

entries.meaning: Causing trouble or extra effort, usually because of bad timing or a bad location. ---
examples: The meeting is at an inconvenient hour for the West Coast.
If Friday is inconvenient for you, we can move it.
They picked the most inconvenient week of the year to repave the street.

entries.meaning: Wrong; not right or not accurate. ---
examples: Three of your answers are incorrect.
The address on the label was incorrect.
He gave an incorrect date for the meeting.
entries.contrast: About behavior, English prefers inappropriate; incorrect is mostly about facts and answers.

entries.meaning: Behaving badly in a way that cannot be changed. ---
examples: He is an incorrigible flirt.
Her son is incorrigible about leaving dishes in the sink.
The judge called him an incorrigible repeat offender.
entries.form: in- + corrigible, from the Latin for correct
entries.contrast: Often affectionate rather than harsh: you are incorrigible can be said with a laugh.

entries.meaning: Impossible to bribe or to talk into doing something dishonest. ---
examples: The city needs an incorruptible inspector.
Everyone agreed the old judge was incorruptible.
He built a reputation as an incorruptible cop.

entries.meaning: Larger than before. ---
examples: Smokers face an increased risk of heart disease.
The bill gives schools increased funding for reading.
Increased demand pushed the price up.
entries.contrast: The verb increase is stressed in-KREESS; the noun is IN-kreess.

entries.meaning: Getting bigger or more frequent. ---
examples: There is increasing pressure on the mayor to resign.
She spoke with increasing confidence as the year went on.
Wildfires arrive with increasing frequency.

entries.meaning: Incredible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The food at that place is incredible.
She did an incredible job on the presentation.
It was the most incredible week of my life.
He told an incredible story about a bear in his kitchen.
The amount of trash they collected is incredible.

senses.head: Extremely good or impressive
examples: The food at that place is incredible.
She did an incredible job on the presentation.
It was the most incredible week of my life.

senses.head: Too strange or extreme to believe
examples: He told an incredible story about a bear in his kitchen.
The amount of trash they collected is incredible.

entries.contrast: Incredible describes the thing; incredulous describes the person who cannot believe it. A story is incredible, a listener is incredulous.

entries.meaning: Unable to believe what you are hearing or seeing. ---
examples: She gave me an incredulous look.
He was incredulous that anyone would pay that much for a bike.
The longer he talked, the more incredulous the jury became.
entries.contrast: Not incredible: a person is incredulous, the news is incredible.

entries.meaning: Happening in small steps rather than all at once. ---
examples: The team made incremental improvements every week.
Reform here is incremental, never dramatic.
We saw an incremental gain of about two percent.

entries.meaning: Making someone look guilty of a crime. ---
examples: Police found incriminating text messages on his phone.
Nothing in the safe was incriminating.
The second video is far more incriminating than the first.

entries.meaning: Incumbent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The incumbent senator is running for a fourth term.
Incumbent mayors rarely lose in this city.
It is incumbent on every driver to check the mirrors.
The court said it was incumbent upon the school to act.

senses.head: Currently holding an office or a job
examples: The incumbent senator is running for a fourth term.
Incumbent mayors rarely lose in this city.

senses.head: Required of someone as a duty
examples: It is incumbent on every driver to check the mirrors.
The court said it was incumbent upon the school to act.

entries.русский: действующий (о должностном лице); лежащий на ком-либо (об обязанности)
entries.takes: on or upon + noun, with a to-infinitive
entries.contrast: Also a noun: the incumbent is the person who currently holds the office.

entries.meaning: Incurable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The disease is serious but not incurable.
He was treated for an incurable form of cancer.
My father is an incurable optimist.
She is an incurable romantic about old houses.

senses.head: Impossible to cure
examples: The disease is serious but not incurable.
He was treated for an incurable form of cancer.

senses.head: Having a habit or quality that will never change
examples: My father is an incurable optimist.
She is an incurable romantic about old houses.

entries.meaning: Indebted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I am indebted to my sister for getting me through that year.
We remain indebted to the volunteers who stayed all night.
No one is more indebted to that teacher than I am.
The plan offers relief to heavily indebted countries.
Many graduates are deeply indebted before their first job.

senses.head: Grateful to someone for their help
examples: I am indebted to my sister for getting me through that year.
We remain indebted to the volunteers who stayed all night.
No one is more indebted to that teacher than I am.

senses.head: Owing a lot of money
examples: The plan offers relief to heavily indebted countries.
Many graduates are deeply indebted before their first job.

entries.position: both — the grateful sense only after a verb
entries.form: from debt — the b is silent

entries.meaning: Offensive, especially about sex or the body. ---
examples: He was arrested for indecent exposure.
The station was fined for broadcasting material far more indecent than that.
They remarried with what the neighbors called indecent haste.
entries.contrast: In law, indecent exposure is a criminal charge. Indecent haste means offensively fast, not improper dress.

entries.meaning: Impossible to read or to work out. ---
examples: The doctor's handwriting is indecipherable.
He left an indecipherable note on the counter.
Half the inscription is worn away and indecipherable.

entries.meaning: Indecisive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is hopelessly indecisive in restaurants.
An indecisive manager slows the whole team down.
She gets more indecisive the more options you give her.
The battle was long and indecisive.
A second indecisive election forced a runoff.

senses.head: Unable to make up your mind
examples: He is hopelessly indecisive in restaurants.
An indecisive manager slows the whole team down.
She gets more indecisive the more options you give her.

senses.head: Not settling anything
examples: The battle was long and indecisive.
A second indecisive election forced a runoff.

entries.meaning: Never getting tired, however long the work goes on. ---
examples: She was an indefatigable campaigner for clean water.
His energy at eighty is indefatigable.
The paper owes the story to one indefatigable reporter.
entries.form: in- + defatigable, from the Latin for tire out

entries.meaning: Impossible to excuse or to argue for. ---
examples: Hitting a child is indefensible.
The company made an indefensible decision to stay quiet.
His conduct that night was indefensible.

entries.meaning: Real, but impossible to put into words. ---
examples: The room had an indefinable smell of old paper.
There is an indefinable sadness in her early songs.
Something about the place is indefinable and hard to leave.

entries.meaning: Indefinite has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The store closed for an indefinite period.
He was put on indefinite leave after the complaint.
Their plans for the summer are still indefinite.
She gave an indefinite answer about the money.

senses.head: With no fixed end or limit
examples: The store closed for an indefinite period.
He was put on indefinite leave after the complaint.

senses.head: Not clear or exact
examples: Their plans for the summer are still indefinite.
She gave an indefinite answer about the money.

entries.contrast: A grammar term as well: a and an are the indefinite articles.

entries.meaning: Indelible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Label the boxes with an indelible marker.
The ink on ballots is indelible on purpose.
That summer left an indelible impression on me.
The photograph is indelible once you have seen it.

senses.head: Impossible to wash off or remove
examples: Label the boxes with an indelible marker.
The ink on ballots is indelible on purpose.

senses.head: Impossible to forget
examples: That summer left an indelible impression on me.
The photograph is indelible once you have seen it.

entries.form: in- + a Latin root meaning blot out

entries.meaning: Slightly rude or embarrassing, especially in what you say. ---
examples: It would be indelicate to ask what she paid for it.
He made an indelicate joke at the reception.
Of all the questions, that was the most indelicate.

entries.meaning: Indented has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Every quotation is indented half an inch.
The first line of each paragraph should be indented.
Maine has a deeply indented coastline.
The leaf has an indented edge.

senses.head: Set in from the margin
examples: Every quotation is indented half an inch.
The first line of each paragraph should be indented.

senses.head: With notches or deep cuts along the edge
examples: Maine has a deeply indented coastline.
The leaf has an indented edge.

entries.meaning: Bound by a contract to work for someone for a fixed number of years. ---
examples: Many colonists arrived as indentured servants.
The plantation ran on indentured labor.
She wrote a book about indentured workers in the Caribbean.
entries.contrast: Nearly always in indentured servant or indentured labor, and nearly always about history.

entries.meaning: Too extreme or too strange for words. ---
examples: The noise in the stadium was indescribable.
She felt an indescribable relief when the phone finally rang.
The smell of that market is indescribable.

entries.meaning: Impossible to break or destroy. ---
examples: The case is advertised as indestructible.
We bought an indestructible chew toy that lasted a week.
Their friendship seemed indestructible.

entries.meaning: Not exactly known or fixed. ---
examples: A man of indeterminate age answered the door.
The soup was an indeterminate shade of brown.
He got an indeterminate sentence of five to ten years.

entries.meaning: Indexed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The book is thoroughly indexed.
Older issues are not indexed online yet.
Benefits are indexed to inflation.
They offered an indexed pension instead of a raise.

senses.head: Provided with an index, or listed in one
examples: The book is thoroughly indexed.
Older issues are not indexed online yet.

senses.head: Tied by a formula to prices, wages or another measure
examples: Benefits are indexed to inflation.
They offered an indexed pension instead of a raise.

entries.meaning: Indicative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A low turnout is indicative of how people feel about the race.
The rash is indicative of an allergy, not an infection.
She works here is in the indicative mood.
Spanish learners meet the indicative long before the subjunctive.

senses.head: Showing or suggesting that something is true
examples: A low turnout is indicative of how people feel about the race.
The rash is indicative of an allergy, not an infection.

senses.head: In grammar, the ordinary mood used for facts and questions
examples: She works here is in the indicative mood.
Spanish learners meet the indicative long before the subjunctive.

entries.position: both — the indicative of sense only after a verb

entries.meaning: Made outside the big studios, labels or publishers. ---
examples: She writes for an indie magazine in Portland.
The theater shows indie films on Tuesdays.
His band started on a tiny indie label.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an indie is an independent film, label or game studio.

entries.meaning: Indifferent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He seemed indifferent to the noise around him.
Voters are not hostile, just indifferent.
The longer the trial went on, the more indifferent the crowd became.
We had an indifferent meal at a place near the station.
After an indifferent start, the team won nine in a row.

senses.head: Not caring about something one way or the other
examples: He seemed indifferent to the noise around him.
Voters are not hostile, just indifferent.
The longer the trial went on, the more indifferent the crowd became.

senses.head: Not very good; ordinary
examples: We had an indifferent meal at a place near the station.
After an indifferent start, the team won nine in a row.

entries.contrast: Not different. Also not the Russian «индифферентный» of chemistry — in everyday English it is about not caring.

entries.meaning: Originally from a particular place rather than brought there. ---
examples: These birds are indigenous to the islands.
The park is replanting indigenous grasses.
The museum was built with Indigenous leaders at the table.
entries.contrast: Capitalized when it refers to peoples: Indigenous communities in Alaska. Of plants and animals it stays lowercase.

entries.meaning: Too poor to pay for basic needs. ---
examples: The county provides a lawyer for indigent defendants.
The clinic treats patients who are indigent or uninsured.
Indigent families qualify for the fee waiver.
entries.contrast: Formal and mostly legal; in ordinary speech Americans say poor or low-income. Also a noun: the indigent.

entries.meaning: Indigestible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Raw beans are indigestible and can make you sick.
The crust was cold and indigestible by then.
The manual is an indigestible block of small print.
He turned an indigestible report into two clear pages.

senses.head: Hard or impossible for the stomach to break down
examples: Raw beans are indigestible and can make you sick.
The crust was cold and indigestible by then.

senses.head: Too dense or dull to take in
examples: The manual is an indigestible block of small print.
He turned an indigestible report into two clear pages.

entries.meaning: Angry because something seems unfair or insulting. ---
examples: She was indignant at being asked to prove she worked there.
He sent an indignant letter to the editor.
The more they explained the fee, the more indignant he got.

entries.meaning: Deep blue with a hint of violet. ---
examples: She wore an indigo dress to the wedding.
The sky over the desert turned indigo.
They still dye the cloth indigo by hand.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the dye and the color: dyed with indigo.

entries.meaning: Indirect has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We took an indirect route to avoid the bridge.
The flight was cheap but indirect.
Stress was an indirect cause of his illness.
She has an indirect way of saying no.
His criticism was more indirect this time.

senses.head: Not going straight from one point to another
examples: We took an indirect route to avoid the bridge.
The flight was cheap but indirect.

senses.head: Not the immediate cause, or not said openly
examples: Stress was an indirect cause of his illness.
She has an indirect way of saying no.
His criticism was more indirect this time.

entries.contrast: A grammar term as well: indirect speech and indirect questions keep statement word order — He asked where I lived.

entries.meaning: Too faint or too slight to be made out. ---
examples: The difference in taste was indiscernible.
At that distance the marks are indiscernible.
The copy is indiscernible from the original.

entries.meaning: Saying or doing something that should have been kept private. ---
examples: One indiscreet remark cost him the job.
It was indiscreet of her to forward that email.
He gets more indiscreet after a second glass of wine.
entries.contrast: Two traps in one word: discreet (tactful) is not discrete (separate), and indiscreet is not indiscrete.

entries.meaning: Done without care about who or what is affected. ---
examples: The report condemns the indiscriminate shelling of villages.
Indiscriminate use of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria.
His reading is wide but indiscriminate.
entries.form: in- + discriminate, in its old sense tell apart

entries.meaning: So necessary that you could not manage without it. ---
examples: A good dictionary is indispensable for translation work.
She made herself indispensable in her first year.
The truck is indispensable to the business.

entries.meaning: Indisposed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The senator is indisposed and will not speak today.
He was indisposed all weekend with a stomach bug.
The bank seems indisposed to lend on those terms.
She was indisposed to discuss it any further.

senses.head: Slightly ill
examples: The senator is indisposed and will not speak today.
He was indisposed all weekend with a stomach bug.

senses.head: Not willing to do something
examples: The bank seems indisposed to lend on those terms.
She was indisposed to discuss it any further.

entries.contrast: Formal and often a polite cover story: she is indisposed can mean anything from a headache to not wanting to come.

entries.meaning: So certain that no one can argue with it. ---
examples: Her talent is indisputable.
The report lays out the indisputable facts first.
It is indisputable that the bridge needs work.

entries.meaning: Hard to see, hear or remember clearly. ---
examples: The shapes in the fog were indistinct.
His voice on the tape is indistinct.
My memory of that day gets more indistinct every year.

entries.meaning: So alike that you cannot tell one from the other. ---
examples: The fake is indistinguishable from the real bill.
The twins were indistinguishable in their school photos.
At that speed the spokes become an indistinguishable blur.

entries.meaning: Individual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Each individual student meets with the adviser once.
The cookies come in individual wrappers.
Teachers here give a lot of individual attention.
The gym writes an individual plan for every member.

senses.head: Single and separate, considered one at a time
examples: Each individual student meets with the adviser once.
The cookies come in individual wrappers.

senses.head: Belonging to or designed for one person
examples: Teachers here give a lot of individual attention.
The gym writes an individual plan for every member.

entries.contrast: Very common as a noun too: an individual is a single person — three individuals were questioned.

entries.meaning: Putting the single person ahead of the group, or doing things your own way. ---
examples: American culture is often called individualistic.
He has an individualistic style that the coach tolerates.
The younger players are more individualistic than the old team was.

entries.meaning: Shaped to fit one particular person. ---
examples: Every student on the plan gets an individualized reading list.
The clinic offers individualized treatment rather than one protocol.
Their training is individualized down to the week.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps -ized; British writing often has individualised.

entries.meaning: Impossible to divide or separate into parts. ---
examples: The pledge calls the nation indivisible.
Seven is indivisible by two.
For her, work and family form one indivisible whole.

entries.meaning: Lazy, in a comfortable and unhurried way. ---
examples: They spent an indolent afternoon by the lake.
The novel follows an indolent young man with too much money.
August makes the whole town more indolent.
entries.contrast: Literary; in speech Americans say lazy. In medicine an indolent tumor is one that grows slowly.

entries.meaning: Impossible to defeat or discourage. ---
examples: She faced the diagnosis with indomitable good humor.
The team's indomitable spirit kept the season alive.
At ninety his will was still indomitable.
entries.form: in- + a Latin root meaning tame

entries.meaning: From Indonesia, or belonging to its people and language. ---
examples: We ate at an Indonesian place near the market.
Indonesian coffee is grown mostly on Sumatra.
Her husband is Indonesian.
entries.contrast: Also a noun — a person, or the language.

entries.meaning: Not open to any doubt. ---
examples: The letters are of indubitable importance to historians.
He is an indubitable master of the short story.
Her right to the money is indubitable.
entries.form: in- + a Latin root meaning doubt
entries.contrast: Formal and slightly old-fashioned; the adverb indubitably is more often met, usually as a joke.

entries.meaning: Caused on purpose by doctors or drugs, or caused by the thing named in a compound. ---
examples: The doctors kept him in an induced coma for three days.
She had an induced labor because the baby was two weeks late.
Many of his health problems are stress-induced.
entries.position: attributive only — alone (induced labor); in compounds also after a verb: The headaches are stress-induced
entries.form: -ed from induce; very often the second half of a compound: drug-induced, stress-induced

entries.meaning: Indulgent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her grandparents are much more indulgent than her parents.
He gave his son an indulgent smile and let him stay up late.
Some teachers think today's parents are too indulgent.
We finished with an indulgent chocolate cake.
A long bath on a weeknight feels wonderfully indulgent.

senses.head: Letting someone have or do whatever they want, often too kindly
examples: Her grandparents are much more indulgent than her parents.
He gave his son an indulgent smile and let him stay up late.
Some teachers think today's parents are too indulgent.

senses.head: Rich and pleasant in a way that feels like a special treat
examples: We finished with an indulgent chocolate cake.
A long bath on a weeknight feels wonderfully indulgent.

entries.meaning: Industrial-strength has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You'll need industrial-strength glue to fix that.
The cleaner is industrial-strength, so wear gloves.
He makes industrial-strength coffee every morning.
It took an industrial-strength effort to get the bill passed.

senses.head: Strong enough to be used in factories or for heavy work
examples: You'll need industrial-strength glue to fix that.
The cleaner is industrial-strength, so wear gloves.

senses.head: Informal: very strong or intense
examples: He makes industrial-strength coffee every morning.
It took an industrial-strength effort to get the bill passed.

entries.meaning: Having a lot of industry and factories. ---
examples: Obesity rates are rising in most industrialized countries.
The north of the country is heavily industrialized.
The US was one of the most industrialized nations in the world by 1900.

entries.meaning: Formal or humorous: drunk. ---
examples: The driver was clearly inebriated when police stopped him.
An inebriated guest fell into the pool.
By midnight, the best man was more inebriated than the groom.

entries.meaning: Not fit to eat, because it is bad, badly cooked or poisonous. ---
examples: The steak was so overcooked it was inedible.
Some of these mushrooms are inedible, so don't pick them.
The cafeteria served an almost inedible meatloaf.
entries.comparison: not gradable — but almost inedible, completely inedible

entries.meaning: Not producing the result that was wanted. ---
examples: Antibiotics are ineffective against viruses.
The new law has been largely ineffective.
The second treatment was even more ineffective than the first.

entries.meaning: Not able to get things done or produce results; weak. ---
examples: Critics called him an ineffectual leader.
Her attempts to calm the crowd were ineffectual.
The committee became more ineffectual every year.
entries.contrast: ineffectual usually describes a person who is weak and cannot get things done (an ineffectual leader); for a method, drug or law, ineffective is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Wasting time, money or energy; not working in the best way. ---
examples: Old refrigerators are very inefficient and use a lot of electricity.
The billing system is slow and inefficient.
It's the most inefficient way to heat a house.
entries.contrast: Russian неэффективный covers two words: ineffective — it does not work; inefficient — it works, but wastes time, money or energy.

entries.meaning: Not graceful, attractive or well done; clumsy. ---
examples: It's an inelegant solution, but it works.
He landed in the water with an inelegant splash.
The new logo is even more inelegant than the old one.

entries.meaning: Not allowed to have or do something because you do not meet the rules. ---
examples: Students who miss the deadline are ineligible for financial aid.
He was ineligible to vote because he was only seventeen.
The team used an ineligible player and lost the game by forfeit.
entries.русский: не имеющий права, не соответствующий условиям

entries.meaning: Having no skill; doing something badly. ---
examples: The robbers were so inept that they locked themselves out of the getaway car.
I'm totally inept at fixing things around the house.
It was the most inept response to a crisis I've ever seen.

entries.meaning: Formal: not fair, especially in the way money or chances are shared. ---
examples: Critics say the tax system is inequitable.
The report describes an inequitable distribution of school funding.
The new rules made an already unfair system even more inequitable.

entries.meaning: Inert has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The man lay inert on the sidewalk until the paramedics arrived.
The economy has been inert for months.
The market was even more inert than analysts had predicted.
Helium is an inert gas.
The pill contains active ingredients and some inert fillers.

senses.head: Not moving or acting; without energy or life
examples: The man lay inert on the sidewalk until the paramedics arrived.
The economy has been inert for months.
The market was even more inert than analysts had predicted.

senses.head: Of a substance, not reacting with other chemicals
examples: Helium is an inert gas.
The pill contains active ingredients and some inert fillers.

entries.comparison: more/most — more inert (the 'not moving' sense); the chemistry sense is not gradable

entries.meaning: Impossible to avoid or ignore. ---
examples: The conclusion is inescapable: the plan failed.
Social media has become an inescapable part of teenage life.
In August, the heat in Phoenix is inescapable.

entries.meaning: Certain to happen; impossible to prevent. ---
examples: Some mistakes are inevitable when you're learning.
It was inevitable that the two companies would merge.
After the scandal, his resignation was almost inevitable.
entries.contrast: the inevitable is also a noun — what cannot be avoided: We tried to delay the inevitable.

entries.meaning: Not completely accurate or correct. ---
examples: Predicting the weather is still an inexact science.
The translation is a little inexact.
Older methods of dating fossils were far more inexact.

entries.meaning: Too bad to be forgiven or explained away. ---
examples: His behavior at the wedding was inexcusable.
Losing the patient's records was an inexcusable mistake.
It's completely inexcusable to leave a dog in a hot car.

entries.meaning: Inexhaustible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sun is an almost inexhaustible source of energy.
Her patience with the kids seemed inexhaustible.
He was an inexhaustible campaigner for civil rights.
At eighty, she is still inexhaustible.

senses.head: So large that it can never be used up
examples: The sun is an almost inexhaustible source of energy.
Her patience with the kids seemed inexhaustible.

senses.head: Of a person, never getting tired
examples: He was an inexhaustible campaigner for civil rights.
At eighty, she is still inexhaustible.

entries.meaning: Formal: impossible to stop or change. ---
examples: Nothing could stop the inexorable rise in prices.
The decline of the small town seemed inexorable.
They watched the inexorable advance of the flood waters.

entries.meaning: Not costing a lot of money. ---
examples: We found an inexpensive little restaurant near the beach.
Rice and beans are healthy and inexpensive.
This is one of the most inexpensive ways to insulate your home.
entries.contrast: inexpensive sounds more positive than cheap, which can also mean 'of poor quality': an inexpensive hotel is a good deal; a cheap hotel may be a bad one.

entries.meaning: Having little knowledge or skill because you have not done something much. ---
examples: The team is young and inexperienced.
An inexperienced driver should not be out in this snow.
She was the most inexperienced candidate in the race.

entries.meaning: Impossible to explain or understand. ---
examples: For some inexplicable reason, the printer only works on Tuesdays.
His sudden decision to quit was inexplicable.
The lights went out for an inexplicable ten minutes.

entries.meaning: Infallible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Doctors aren't infallible.
He speaks as if his judgment were infallible.
There's no infallible way to pick stocks.
Grandma had an infallible cure for hiccups.

examples: The security screening felt invasive.
She asked a few invasive questions about my salary.

entries.position: both — an invasive species; the test is invasive

entries.meaning: Good at thinking up new ideas or new ways of doing things. ---
examples: The chef here is remarkably inventive.
It is an inventive solution to a very old problem.
Her second novel is more inventive than the first.
entries.position: both — an inventive solution; the chef is inventive

entries.meaning: Moving in the opposite direction, so that one goes up as the other goes down. ---
examples: There is an inverse relationship between price and demand.
Attendance fell in inverse proportion to ticket prices.
The two effects are inverse to each other.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an inverse relationship; the two effects are inverse to each other
entries.contrast: The inverse is also a noun in math, and there the stress moves forward: IN-vurs.

entries.meaning: Turned upside down, or put into the opposite order. ---
examples: News stories use an inverted pyramid structure.
The image in the mirror is inverted.
He wore an inverted cross on a chain.
entries.position: both — an inverted pyramid; the image is inverted

entries.meaning: Doing or involving careful digging into facts, especially where something has gone wrong. ---
examples: She won a prize for investigative journalism.
The investigative team spent a year on the story.
He heads the bureau's investigative division.

entries.meaning: Having to do with an official investigation. ---
examples: The committee has broad investigatory powers.
The agency opened an investigatory file on the company.
Her lawyers challenged the board's investigatory process.
entries.contrast: investigative is the everyday word; investigatory turns up mostly in legal writing about official powers and procedures.

entries.meaning: Having done something for so long that it will never change. ---
examples: He is an inveterate gambler.
My uncle is an inveterate storyteller.
She is an inveterate collector of old maps.
entries.contrast: It goes with a person and a long-standing habit, usually a bad one: an inveterate liar. You cannot say the habit is inveterate about a person.

entries.meaning: Unfair in a way that is bound to offend someone or stir up bad feeling. ---
examples: It would be invidious to name only three of them.
He drew an invidious comparison between the two sisters.
The ranking puts her in an invidious position.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an invidious comparison; it would be invidious to choose

entries.meaning: Filled with fresh energy and strength. ---
examples: I always feel invigorated after a swim.
She came back from vacation invigorated.
The crowd left the team invigorated for the second half.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: I felt invigorated

entries.meaning: Giving you fresh energy. ---
examples: The cold morning air was invigorating.
She took an invigorating walk before breakfast.
Nothing is more invigorating than a swim in the lake.
entries.position: both — an invigorating walk; the cold air was invigorating

entries.meaning: Impossible to beat or defeat. ---
examples: At seventeen you feel invincible.
The team looked invincible all season.
No army is truly invincible.
entries.position: both — an invincible army; the team looked invincible

entries.meaning: That must never be broken, attacked or interfered with. ---
examples: They treat that rule as inviolable.
The constitution calls these rights inviolable.
Sunday dinner at Grandma's was an inviolable tradition.
entries.position: both — an inviolable rule; these rights are inviolable

entries.meaning: Invisible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Invisible ink shows up under a black light.
The crack is nearly invisible from the street.
Radio waves are invisible to us.
She felt invisible at the party.
Night-shift workers are invisible to most of the company.

senses.head: Impossible to see
examples: Invisible ink shows up under a black light.
The crack is nearly invisible from the street.
Radio waves are invisible to us.

senses.head: Present but ignored, as if nobody could see you
examples: She felt invisible at the party.
Night-shift workers are invisible to most of the company.

entries.position: both — invisible ink; the crack is invisible

entries.meaning: Attractive enough to make you want to come in, sit down or try it. ---
examples: The kitchen smelled warm and inviting.
The lake looked inviting on a day like that.
Their new lobby is much more inviting than the old one.
entries.position: both — an inviting room; the water looked inviting

entries.meaning: Involuntary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Blinking is an involuntary movement.
She gave an involuntary gasp when the lights went out.
He faces involuntary commitment to a hospital.
Most of the layoffs were involuntary.

senses.head: Happening by itself, without your choosing it
examples: Blinking is an involuntary movement.
She gave an involuntary gasp when the lights went out.

senses.head: Forced on someone who did not agree to it
examples: He faces involuntary commitment to a hospital.
Most of the layoffs were involuntary.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an involuntary gasp; the layoffs were involuntary

entries.meaning: Impossible to harm, attack or damage. ---
examples: No system is invulnerable to attack.
He acted as though he were invulnerable.
They built an invulnerable lead by halftime.
entries.position: both — an invulnerable position; no system is invulnerable

entries.meaning: Turned toward the inside, or belonging to your private thoughts. ---
examples: The novel describes a long inward journey.
She gave an inward groan and kept smiling.
The latch needs a short inward push to release.
entries.contrast: inward is also an adverb — the door swings inward — and Americans also say inwards for the adverb. The adjective only goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Treated with iodine. ---
examples: Use iodized salt unless the recipe says otherwise.
Iodized salt prevents a common thyroid problem.
The store carries only iodized table salt.
entries.form: from iodine, the element added to it

entries.meaning: From Iran, or having to do with Iran. ---
examples: We ate at a new Iranian restaurant downtown.
She studies Iranian film at the university.
His parents are Iranian.
entries.position: both — an Iranian film; her parents are Iranian
entries.contrast: An Iranian is also a noun for a person from Iran. Persian usually names the language and the older culture, not the modern country. Always capitalized.

entries.meaning: From Iraq, or having to do with Iraq. ---
examples: He met an Iraqi family at the clinic.
The Iraqi government issued a statement this morning.
Her husband is Iraqi.
entries.position: both — the Iraqi government; her husband is Iraqi
entries.contrast: An Iraqi is also a noun for a person from Iraq. Always capitalized.

entries.meaning: Quick to lose your temper over small things. ---
examples: The old man was famously irascible.
He gets more irascible every year.
She plays an irascible judge in the series.
entries.position: both — an irascible old man; he gets irascible when he's tired

entries.meaning: Very angry. ---
examples: An irate customer demanded a refund.
The neighbors were irate about the noise.
She wrote an irate letter to the editor.
entries.position: both — an irate customer; the neighbors were irate

entries.meaning: Showing shifting rainbow colors as the light or the angle changes. ---
examples: The beetle's shell is iridescent.
She wore an iridescent green dress.
Soap bubbles look iridescent in the sun.
entries.position: both — an iridescent shell; the bubbles are iridescent

entries.meaning: So firm that nothing can break it or get around it. ---
examples: We offer an ironclad guarantee on parts and labor.
His alibi was ironclad.
They signed an ironclad contract.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an ironclad guarantee; his alibi was ironclad
entries.contrast: The literal sense, 'armored with iron', survives mostly in an ironclad warship and in the noun an ironclad.

entries.meaning: Ironic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His tone was ironic, not sincere.
She made an ironic remark about the weather.
It is ironic that the fire station burned down.
In an ironic twist, he ended up working for the company he sued.

senses.head: Saying the opposite of what you mean, to be funny or cutting
examples: His tone was ironic, not sincere.
She made an ironic remark about the weather.

senses.head: Odd in a way that seems like a joke played by fate
examples: It is ironic that the fire station burned down.
In an ironic twist, he ended up working for the company he sued.

entries.position: both — an ironic smile; it's ironic that he lost

entries.meaning: Not based on reason or clear thinking. ---
examples: She has an irrational fear of bridges.
He gets irrational when he hasn't slept.
The more he drank, the more irrational he became.
entries.position: both — an irrational fear; he gets irrational when he's tired
entries.form: ir- (the form of in- before r) + rational

entries.meaning: So different that they can never be brought into agreement. ---
examples: They divorced over irreconcilable differences.
The two versions of the story are irreconcilable.
His account is irreconcilable with the video.
entries.position: both — irreconcilable differences; the two accounts are irreconcilable

entries.meaning: Too bad to be fixed, saved or forgiven. ---
examples: The script isn't irredeemable — it just needs work.
He wrote the whole season off as irredeemable.
She doesn't believe anyone is irredeemable.
entries.position: both — an irredeemable mess; nobody is irredeemable

entries.meaning: Impossible to argue against or disprove. ---
examples: The DNA evidence was irrefutable.
He made an irrefutable case for the change.
The logic here is irrefutable.
entries.position: both — irrefutable evidence; the logic is irrefutable
entries.contrast: Also commonly said ih-REF-yuh-tuh-buhl, with the stress pulled back to the second syllable.

entries.meaning: Irregular has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He keeps irregular hours.
Her heartbeat was irregular, so they kept her overnight.
The patio is laid with stones of irregular shapes.
The coastline here is wild and irregular.
Go is an irregular verb.
The hiring process was highly irregular.

senses.head: Not happening at even intervals
examples: He keeps irregular hours.
Her heartbeat was irregular, so they kept her overnight.

senses.head: Not even or smooth in shape or surface
examples: The patio is laid with stones of irregular shapes.
The coastline here is wild and irregular.

senses.head: Not following the usual rule or the proper procedure
examples: Go is an irregular verb.
The hiring process was highly irregular.

entries.position: both — an irregular heartbeat; the shape is irregular

entries.meaning: Having nothing to do with the matter being discussed. ---
examples: That fact is irrelevant to the case.
The judge ruled the question irrelevant.
His age is completely irrelevant here.
entries.position: both — an irrelevant question; his age is irrelevant

entries.meaning: Too badly damaged to be repaired or put right. ---
examples: The flood did irreparable damage to the archive.
His reputation suffered irreparable harm.
The argument caused an irreparable break between the brothers.
entries.position: attributive only — irreparable damage; after a verb say beyond repair
entries.contrast: The stress falls on -REP-, not on -PAIR-: ih-REP-ur-uh-buhl, even though it comes from repair.

entries.meaning: So rare or so special that nothing else could take its place. ---
examples: Those family photographs are irreplaceable.
She is an irreplaceable part of this office.
The fire destroyed irreplaceable records.
entries.position: both — an irreplaceable coach; those photos are irreplaceable

entries.meaning: So full of energy or good spirits that nothing can hold it back. ---
examples: Her irrepressible laugh carried across the room.
He is an irrepressible optimist.
The puppy is irrepressible before breakfast.
entries.position: both — an irrepressible optimist; the puppy is irrepressible

entries.meaning: So correct that nobody can find fault with it. ---
examples: Her conduct during the investigation was irreproachable.
He has an irreproachable record after thirty years on the job.
The hotel's service is irreproachable.

entries.meaning: Irresistible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dessert menu was irresistible.
She has an almost irresistible smile.
The offer was irresistible to a kid who had never flown before.
He felt an irresistible urge to laugh.
By spring the case for reform had become irresistible.

senses.head: So attractive or tempting that you cannot say no
examples: The dessert menu was irresistible.
She has an almost irresistible smile.
The offer was irresistible to a kid who had never flown before.

senses.head: Too strong to be stopped or held back
examples: He felt an irresistible urge to laugh.
By spring the case for reform had become irresistible.

entries.contrast: Spelled -ible, not -able.

entries.meaning: Not thinking about the harm your actions may do. ---
examples: It was irresponsible to leave the kids alone.
He is a nice guy, but completely irresponsible with money.
Printing a rumor like that is irresponsible journalism.

entries.meaning: Impossible to get back or to put right again. ---
examples: The fire did irretrievable damage to the archive.
Deleted files are not always irretrievable.
The court found an irretrievable breakdown of the marriage.

entries.meaning: Making fun of things other people treat as serious or sacred. ---
examples: The show takes an irreverent look at Washington.
His humor is irreverent but never cruel.
Some readers found the cartoon irreverent.

entries.meaning: Impossible to change back to how it was. ---
examples: The damage to her hearing is irreversible.
Scientists warn of irreversible changes to the coastline.
Once you sign, the decision is irreversible.

entries.meaning: Final, so that it cannot be canceled or taken back. ---
examples: The offer is irrevocable for thirty days.
She made an irrevocable decision to leave the company.
The bank issued an irrevocable letter of credit.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable — i-REV-uh-kuh-buhl, not on -voke.

entries.meaning: Easily annoyed, usually because of tiredness or stress. ---
examples: He gets irritable when he is hungry.
After three hours of sleep she was irritable all morning.
Do not take it personally — he is just in an irritable mood.
entries.contrast: Irritable is the person's mood; irritating is the thing that causes it.

entries.meaning: Belonging to Islam or to the countries where it is the main religion. ---
examples: Islamic art fills two rooms of the museum.
She teaches a course on Islamic law.
The mosque is a landmark of Islamic architecture.

entries.meaning: Isolated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They live on an isolated farm in Montana.
After the move she felt isolated and homesick.
The police called it an isolated incident.
There were isolated reports of flooding in the valley.

senses.head: Far from other places or other people
examples: They live on an isolated farm in Montana.
After the move she felt isolated and homesick.

senses.head: Happening only once, not part of a pattern
examples: The police called it an isolated incident.
There were isolated reports of flooding in the valley.

entries.meaning: Wanting a country to stay out of other countries' affairs. ---
examples: He ran on an isolationist foreign policy.
Isolationist sentiment grew through the 1930s.
The party took an isolationist turn after the war.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: the isolationists in Congress.

entries.meaning: Isometric has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The physical therapist gave her isometric exercises.
Isometric training builds strength without movement.
The plans use an isometric projection.
He drew the room in isometric view.

senses.head: Of exercise, working the muscle without moving the joint
examples: The physical therapist gave her isometric exercises.
Isometric training builds strength without movement.

senses.head: Of a drawing, showing three sides at equal angles
examples: The plans use an isometric projection.
He drew the room in isometric view.

entries.meaning: Of a triangle, having two sides of equal length. ---
examples: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides.
Draw an isosceles triangle with a four-inch base.
The roof forms a nearly perfect isosceles triangle.

entries.meaning: Of type, sloping to the right. ---
examples: Book titles go in italic type.
Use an italic font for the quotations.
The italic letters are hard to read at that size.
entries.contrast: The noun is normally plural: set the title in italics.

entries.meaning: Feeling an unpleasant tickle on the skin, or causing one. ---
examples: My eyes get itchy every spring.
That wool sweater is itchy.
The rash is itchier at night than during the day.

entries.meaning: Done by repeating a cycle and improving it each time. ---
examples: The team uses an iterative design process.
The algorithm takes an iterative approach to the answer.
Writing is iterative — you draft, you cut, you draft again.

entries.meaning: Traveling from place to place to work. ---
examples: He was an itinerant preacher in the 1930s.
Itinerant workers followed the harvest north.
She spent ten years as an itinerant musician.

entries.meaning: Very small. ---
examples: There is an itsy-bitsy spider in the tub.
She wore an itsy-bitsy yellow polka-dot bikini.
He left me an itsy-bitsy piece of cake.
entries.contrast: Baby talk or a joke; the neutral word is tiny.

entries.meaning: Very small.
examples: They live in an itty-bitty apartment downtown.
The puppy was an itty-bitty thing when we got him.
I only had an itty-bitty taste of it.
